title: The Goose-Girl (Die Gänsemagd)

full_text:
A beautiful royal princess was betrothed to a king's son in a distant land. When the time came for her bridal journey, her loving mother gave her a handkerchief marked with three drops of maternal blood for protection, and a magnificent talking horse named Falada. She was accompanied by a treacherous maid-in-waiting.

On the long journey across parched plains, the princess asked the maid to fetch her a cup of water from the brook. The maid arrogantly refused: "I will not serve you any longer; climb down and drink yourself!" In her distress, the princess dropped her handkerchief into the stream, losing her mother's blessing.

Taking advantage of her weakness, the cruel maid forced the princess to trade dresses, switch horses, and swear a solemn oath beneath the open sky never to reveal the betrayal to any mortal living soul. At the palace, the false bride was received in grand splendor, while the real princess was sent into the meadows to herd geese alongside a boy named Conrad.

Fearing the horse would speak, the wicked maid ordered Falada beheaded. But the gentle princess begged the knacker to nail the horse's head over the dark city gateway, where she passed every morning. As she walked beneath, she sighed: "Alas, Falada, hanging there!" and the horse answered: "Alas, young queen, how sad your share! If your dear mother only knew, her loving heart would break in two."

Conrad grew furious when the princess untied her golden hair in the meadow, gleaming like the sun, and the wind blew his hat away whenever he tried to steal a strand. He complained to the old king, who observed the girl and saw her deep sorrow.

When the king questioned her, she wept that she had sworn never to tell her grief to any mortal. The wise old king said: "If you cannot speak to me, pour out your heart to the iron stove in the corner."

The princess crawled into the warm iron stove and poured forth her whole tragic story of treachery and suffering. The king, listening through the flue pipe outside, heard every word. He clothed her in royal silk, summoned a magnificent feast, and asked the false bride what punishment a traitor deserved. The wicked maid condemned herself out of her own mouth, and the true queen was restored to her rightful throne beside her joyful prince.
moral: True nobility cannot be stolen, and the quiet truth will always triumph over deceit.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Goose-Girl (Die Gänsemagd)"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
